paragraph_predictions.paragraph:
Primary brain tumor detection in computer-aided diagnosis systems is increasingly driven by neural networks applied to medical imaging, especially MRI and, in some cases, CT scans. Across the cited works, the dominant pattern is the use of deep learning models—most commonly CNNs and transfer-learning architectures such as VGG16, ResNet50, Xception, MobileNet, EfficientNet, DenseNet, and custom lightweight CNNs—to classify tumors into categories such as glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumor, and non-tumor, or to perform binary tumor/non-tumor detection. These systems are positioned as decision-support tools for radiologists and clinicians, aiming to reduce manual workload, speed diagnosis, and improve consistency.

A common technical pipeline emerges. Medical images are first preprocessed using resizing, normalization, contrast enhancement, histogram equalization, denoising, filtering, and sometimes segmentation or wavelet transforms. Many studies emphasize data augmentation—rotation, flipping, zooming, brightness and contrast changes—to improve generalization and reduce overfitting when datasets are small or imbalanced. Feature handling varies by approach: some methods rely on end-to-end CNN feature learning, while others combine handcrafted statistical, texture, PCA, wavelet, GLCM, or other engineered features with neural classifiers or SVMs. Hybrid designs, such as wavelet-CNN, PSO-CNN, or feature-based deep networks, are presented as ways to improve efficiency and capture clinically relevant patterns.

Transfer learning is one of the strongest recurring themes. Pre-trained models adapted from natural image datasets are reported to reduce training time, improve convergence, and perform well even with limited labeled brain imaging data. Architectural enhancements such as dropout, batch normalization, attention mechanisms, dense connectivity, separable convolutions, and lightweight layers are frequently used to improve robustness and computational efficiency. Some studies extend beyond classification into segmentation using U-Net-like models, multimodal MRI fusion, or multi-modal inputs such as T1, T1ce, T2, and FLAIR, which can improve detection by combining complementary anatomical information.

The literature also highlights system-level CAD capabilities. Several works describe complete platforms that include web or cloud deployment, graphical interfaces, clinical data integration, multimodal image support, decision support workflows, hospital information system compatibility, and even location-based care recommendations. Explainable AI methods such as Grad-CAM and SHAP are increasingly incorporated to visualize model attention and improve trust, while privacy-preserving and scalable approaches such as federated learning, SaaS deployment, big-data frameworks like Spark, and secure IoMT transmission are proposed for real-world deployment.

Overall, the field suggests that neural-network-based CAD systems for primary brain tumor detection are effective and rapidly maturing. They show strong performance in tumor classification and segmentation, especially when supported by preprocessing, augmentation, transfer learning, and explainability. However, recurring challenges remain: limited annotated datasets, class imbalance, overfitting, variability in imaging protocols, interpretability, computational cost, and the need for broader clinical validation. Even so, the combined evidence indicates substantial promise for these systems as practical medical imaging tools for early and reliable primary brain tumor diagnosis.

paragraph_predictions.paragraph:
Summary: Primary Brain Tumor Detection Using Computer-Aided Neural Network Systems

Computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) systems for primary brain tumor detection and classification increasingly use neural networks to analyze medical images, particularly MRI scans. Typical approaches combine image preprocessing, feature extraction, classification, and explainability to distinguish tumor types or separate tumor from non-tumor cases.

A common strategy is transfer learning, where pretrained convolutional neural networks such as ResNet, VGG, Xception, EfficientNet, DenseNet, or MobileNet extract informative features from MRI images. These representations can either feed conventional classification layers or specialized classifiers. Preprocessing and augmentation, including normalization, resizing, rotation, flipping, contrast adjustment, and noise reduction, are frequently used to improve robustness and reduce overfitting when annotated medical datasets are limited.

The supplied literature describes PBTNet as one such CAD architecture. It reportedly uses a pretrained ResNet-18 for feature extraction, followed by an ensemble of three randomized neural networks: a Schmidt neural network, random vector functional-link network, and extreme learning machine. Their predictions are combined through majority voting, with the intended benefit of improving classification robustness and accuracy. The reported system also employs Grad-CAM to visualize image regions influencing predictions, providing clinicians with an interpretable indication of where the network is focusing.

More broadly, the supplied studies suggest several recurring directions in brain-tumor CAD research:

Transfer learning can reduce training requirements when medical datasets are relatively small.
CNN-based feature learning can reduce reliance on manually designed image features.
Ensemble learning can combine complementary classifiers to potentially improve robustness.
Data augmentation and regularization are commonly used to address overfitting and limited training samples.
Explainable AI, particularly Grad-CAM and related techniques, can provide spatial explanations of neural-network decisions.
Segmentation architectures such as U-Net can complement classification by locating tumor regions at the pixel level.
Lightweight architectures such as MobileNet or separable-convolution networks may facilitate deployment where computational resources are constrained.
Important retraction caveat

The supplied metadata explicitly identifies “PBTNet: a new computer-aided diagnosis system for detecting primary brain tumors” as a retracted paper. Consequently, its reported architecture, performance, sensitivity, accuracy, robustness, transfer-learning benefits, and Grad-CAM results should not be treated as reliable scientific evidence or used to substantiate conclusions about clinical effectiveness.

The PBTNet claims can still be discussed when describing what the retracted publication reported, but they should be clearly labeled as originating from a retracted source. The broader conclusion supported by the non-retracted material provided here is that neural-network CAD for brain-tumor imaging is an active approach encompassing transfer learning, CNN feature extraction, ensembles, preprocessing, segmentation, and explainability. However, claims of clinical diagnostic effectiveness require independent validation on representative external datasets and should not be inferred from a retracted study or high retrospective classification accuracy alone.

paragraph_predictions.paragraph:
Transfer learning with pre-trained convolutional neural networks (CNNs), combined with explainability methods such as Grad-CAM, can improve automated brain tumor detection and classification from MRI scans in two complementary ways: transfer learning reduces the amount of labeled medical data needed to build an effective classifier, while explainability makes its predictions easier to inspect and interpret.

Transfer learning can help when labeled MRI data are limited

Rather than training a CNN entirely from scratch, transfer learning starts with a network that has already learned useful image representations and adapts it to brain MRI classification.

Pre-trained architectures including VGG16, ResNet50, MobileNet, and Xception have been used to classify MRI scans into categories such as glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumor, and no tumor.
The supplied studies indicate that transfer learning can improve classification performance and generalization while reducing training time and the requirement for extensive labeled medical datasets.
In particular, the Xception-based work reports that transfer learning from natural-image datasets helps the network adapt to brain MRI analysis and reduces its dependence on large labeled medical-imaging datasets. Similarly, fine-tuned ResNet50 is reported to improve classification when labeled medical data are limited.
Transfer learning can also be combined with dropout, batch normalization, and fine-tuning to reduce overfitting and stabilize training.

This is especially relevant because the supplied literature identifies scarcity of large annotated datasets as an important obstacle in brain-tumor imaging.

Preprocessing and augmentation complement transfer learning

Transfer learning alone does not eliminate problems caused by small datasets. The supplied claims consistently identify normalization, resizing, augmentation, and noise reduction as useful complementary measures.

For example, rotations, flips, zooming, and brightness or contrast changes can expose the network to greater image variability without requiring additional labeled scans. These approaches are reported to improve robustness and generalization and reduce overfitting. Dropout and batch normalization provide additional regularization.

Thus, a limited-data workflow supported by the supplied evidence is conceptually:

MRI preprocessing → data augmentation → pre-trained CNN → fine-tuning/classification → explainability

Grad-CAM can make CNN decisions more transparent

Grad-CAM addresses a different limitation of CNN-based diagnosis: lack of interpretability.

The supplied evidence indicates that Grad-CAM produces region-based visual explanations that highlight areas of an MRI scan that contributed most strongly to a tumor classification. This allows a user to inspect whether the network's attention is concentrated on plausible tumor regions rather than treating the classification as an unexplained output.

The supplied work on explainable brain-tumor classification further suggests that:

Grad-CAM can provide spatial explanations of predictions.
SHAP can complement Grad-CAM by providing pixel-level feature-importance information.
Using Grad-CAM and SHAP together can improve the interpretability and perceived trustworthiness of predictions.
Examining explanations for misclassified cases can reveal possible biases in model attention or feature reliance, providing information that can be used to improve the classifier.
Overall

The evidence therefore supports a complementary strategy. Transfer learning addresses the data-efficiency problem by reusing learned image features and fine-tuning them for MRI classification, while Grad-CAM addresses the transparency problem by showing which image regions influenced a prediction. Data augmentation, normalization, dropout, batch normalization, and careful fine-tuning can further mitigate overfitting when training samples are scarce.

Together, these methods can make automated MRI brain-tumor systems more data-efficient, robust, and interpretable, potentially strengthening their usefulness as decision-support tools for medical professionals. However, the supplied material also identifies continuing issues including class imbalance, imaging-protocol variability, computational requirements, model bias, and limited annotated datasets. Explainability therefore provides a way to inspect model behavior rather than, by itself, establishing that a prediction is clinically correct.

Evidence note: PBTNet: a new computer-aided diagnosis system for detecting primary brain tumors is listed in the supplied metadata as retracted, so its claims should not be used as reliable supporting evidence. The conclusions above are supported by the other, non-retracted material provided.

Visual explanation techniques can make CNN-based brain-tumor detection more interpretable by showing which parts or features of an MRI contributed to a prediction, rather than presenting only a tumor label or confidence score.

Localize the evidence behind a prediction. Grad-CAM can highlight MRI regions that are most relevant to a CNN's tumor classification. This provides a spatial explanation that can help a clinician see whether the model is focusing on a plausible tumor region rather than treating the network as a purely opaque classifier.

Provide complementary levels of explanation. The supplied evidence describes Grad-CAM as giving region-level explanations, while SHAP provides pixel-level feature importance. Combining these approaches can therefore show both where the model is concentrating and which image features contribute to its decision.

Expose questionable model behavior. Grad-CAM and SHAP can be applied to misclassified cases to reveal potential biases in model attention or feature reliance. Such analysis provides actionable information for identifying and improving problematic behavior rather than relying solely on aggregate accuracy, precision, or recall.

Increase transparency and potential clinical trust. Lack of model interpretability is identified in the supplied material as a barrier to clinical deployment. Visual explanations directly address this limitation by making the basis of a CNN prediction more inspectable. The cited claims consequently associate explainable methods with greater transparency, trustworthiness, and potential clinical adoption.

Support, rather than replace, diagnostic judgment. The broader supplied evidence presents CNN-based tumor classifiers as potential clinical decision-support tools. In that context, an explanation map can accompany a classification such as glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumor, or no tumor, giving healthcare professionals additional information with which to interpret the model's output. Segmentation approaches can further provide pixel-level tumor localization and clinically relevant information such as volumetric analysis.

Overall, the strongest conclusion supported by the supplied claims is that visual explanation methods can turn a CNN prediction from an isolated classification into a spatially interpretable result. Grad-CAM identifies influential image regions, feature-attribution approaches such as SHAP provide finer-grained importance information, and their combination can help clinicians inspect predictions and investigators diagnose model errors or biases. This improves the potential clinical usefulness of CNNs by addressing transparency and interpretability, while the supplied claims do not establish that explanation maps themselves guarantee diagnostic correctness or clinical validity.

Decentralized access control in IoT blockchain smart contract–based auditable systems centers on replacing centralized authentication and authorization servers with distributed ledgers and programmable smart contracts. Across the cited works, the common architecture uses layered designs with IoT devices at the edge, gateway or edge nodes to offload heavy computation, a permissioned or consortium blockchain layer for trust and coordination, and application or cloud layers for services and storage. This structure is repeatedly presented as a practical way to secure resource-constrained IoT environments while avoiding single points of failure and improving resilience, trust, and transparency.

A consistent theme is that smart contracts act as the policy enforcement engine for decentralized access control. They automate authentication, authorization, delegation, revocation, and real-time permission updates without relying on a central authority. Different models appear in the literature, including role-based access control, attribute-based access control, hybrid RBAC-ABAC schemes, context-aware access control, zero-trust policies, and even lattice-based multi-level security. Several frameworks extend access decisions beyond static roles by incorporating contextual factors such as time, location, user purpose, operating environment, device status, and risk level. This makes blockchain-enabled IoT access control not only decentralized, but also dynamic and fine-grained.

Auditability is one of the strongest benefits emphasized across the studies. Because blockchain provides immutable, timestamped, and tamper-evident logs, every access request, policy update, identity event, and data-sharing transaction can be recorded in a verifiable manner. This supports accountability, forensic analysis, compliance, and trust among multiple stakeholders. In sectors such as healthcare, industrial IoT, smart homes, smart cities, agriculture, and academic repositories, this audit trail is presented as a major advantage over centralized systems, where logs can be altered, hidden, or controlled by a single administrator.

To make these systems practical for IoT, many frameworks avoid storing raw sensor data directly on-chain. Instead, they store hashes, access metadata, permissions, identifiers, and audit records on-chain, while placing encrypted data in off-chain storage such as cloud platforms or IPFS. This hybrid design preserves integrity and traceability while reducing blockchain storage costs, computational overhead, and latency. Gateways, edge nodes, and coordinators are commonly used to shield constrained IoT devices from expensive blockchain operations. Some proposals also introduce lightweight cryptography, efficient consensus methods such as PoA, PoS, PBFT, or reputation-assisted voting, and scaling techniques like sidechains, sharding, and hybrid public-private chains.

Another major pattern is the integration of decentralized identity management with access control. Blockchain frameworks often use device, service, and user identities supported by cryptographic credentials, decentralized identifiers, verifiable credentials, PKI, ECC, or privacy-preserving methods such as zero-knowledge proofs. This strengthens device authentication and reduces dependence on centralized identity providers. In more advanced systems, AI, federated learning, anomaly detection, and risk scoring are combined with blockchain logging and smart contracts to support adaptive or context-sensitive access decisions and continuous monitoring.

Overall, the literature suggests that decentralized access control for IoT using blockchain and smart contracts offers strong advantages in tamper resistance, transparency, distributed trust, automated enforcement, fine-grained policy control, and auditable operation. The most mature designs are permissioned or consortium-based, use off-chain encrypted storage, and rely on gateways or edge computing for efficiency. At the same time, recurring open challenges include scalability, latency, interoperability across platforms, metadata privacy, key management, regulatory compliance, and energy efficiency. Even so, the consensus across the provided studies is that blockchain-smart contract architectures are a promising foundation for auditable, trustworthy, and decentralized IoT access control systems.

The literature presented around decentralized IoT access control converges on blockchain and smart contracts as mechanisms for replacing centralized authorization services with distributed, tamper-resistant, and auditable security architectures. In these systems, blockchain typically provides an immutable record of identities, policies, permissions, and access events, while smart contracts automate authentication, authorization, delegation, revocation, and context-dependent policy enforcement. This combination can reduce single points of failure and make security decisions independently verifiable.

A recurring architectural pattern separates resource-constrained IoT devices from blockchain operations. Gateways, edge nodes, or other intermediaries handle computationally intensive consensus, cryptography, and ledger interactions. Sensitive or high-volume IoT data is commonly retained off-chain, for example in cloud storage or IPFS, with hashes, identifiers, permissions, and limited metadata recorded on-chain. This hybrid approach seeks to preserve blockchain's integrity and auditability benefits without requiring devices to store or process the entire ledger.

Access-control mechanisms range from role-based and attribute-based models to context-aware and adaptive authorization. Smart contracts can evaluate roles, identities, device attributes, time, location, purpose, operating conditions, or risk information before granting access. More advanced proposals combine blockchain with decentralized identifiers, verifiable credentials, zero-knowledge techniques, federated learning, AI-based anomaly detection, or zero-trust principles. Collectively, these approaches aim to provide finer-grained authorization while preserving privacy and accommodating changing IoT environments.

Auditability is one of the principal advantages of this design paradigm. Authentication attempts, authorization decisions, permission changes, and other security events can be cryptographically linked to an append-only distributed ledger. This creates a traceable history that is significantly harder for an individual administrator or compromised service to alter retrospectively. Permissioned or consortium blockchains are particularly prominent because IoT deployments often involve identifiable organizations and require stronger governance, privacy, and performance guarantees than unrestricted public networks.

At the same time, blockchain does not automatically solve IoT security. The supplied studies repeatedly identify trade-offs involving transaction latency, throughput, storage, energy consumption, interoperability, privacy of blockchain metadata, key management, and consensus overhead. Proposed mitigations include lightweight or permissioned consensus protocols, gateway and edge processing, hybrid public/private blockchains, off-chain storage, sidechains, sharding, and lightweight cryptography.

Overall, the material suggests a general architecture in which IoT devices generate or consume resources, gateways or edge infrastructure mediate blockchain interaction, smart contracts make or enforce authorization decisions, and the blockchain maintains a tamper-evident audit trail. Such systems can strengthen decentralization, accountability, transparency, and resilience, but practical effectiveness depends heavily on careful choices of consensus mechanism, identity management, privacy safeguards, storage architecture, and policy design.

Cardiac arrhythmia detection using **dual-tree wavelet transform and convolutional neural networks (CNNs)** is a hybrid approach that combines powerful signal preprocessing with automatic deep feature learning.

### Core idea
- **Dual-tree complex wavelet transform (DTCWT)** is used to preprocess ECG signals and extract informative time-frequency characteristics.
- **CNNs** then learn discriminative patterns from these transformed signals or derived features to classify arrhythmias automatically.

### Why dual-tree wavelet transform is useful
Compared with standard discrete wavelet transform (DWT), DTCWT is often preferred because it:
- provides better shift invariance,
- preserves directional and oscillatory information more effectively,
- produces lower energy discrepancy in coefficients,
- improves robustness to ECG noise and morphological variation.

In arrhythmia analysis, DTCWT helps with:
- **denoising** ECG signals,
- reducing **baseline wander**, **powerline interference**, and **muscle noise**,
- enhancing clinically important waveform components such as the **P wave, QRS complex, and T wave**,
- supporting segmentation and feature extraction for abnormal beat detection.

### Role of CNNs
CNNs reduce or eliminate the need for manual feature engineering by learning features directly from:
- raw ECG beats,
- wavelet coefficient sequences,
- or 2D time-frequency representations generated from wavelet transforms.

These networks have been used for:
- multi-class arrhythmia classification,
- inter-patient heartbeat classification,
- premature ventricular contraction detection,
- atrial fibrillation detection.

CNN-based systems are particularly effective because they can capture:
- local morphological changes in ECG waveforms,
- temporal context across adjacent beats,
- multi-scale patterns revealed by wavelet decomposition.

### Combined framework
A typical DTCWT-CNN arrhythmia pipeline includes:
1. **ECG acquisition**
2. **Preprocessing and denoising** using wavelet-based filtering, often DTCWT
3. **Beat detection/segmentation**, often around R-peaks
4. **Feature representation**, either:
   - handcrafted from DTCWT coefficients, or
   - passed directly to a CNN
5. **CNN classification** into arrhythmia categories such as normal, supraventricular ectopic, ventricular ectopic, or atrial fibrillation

Some related studies also combine wavelet processing with:
- attention mechanisms,
- dual-path CNNs,
- focal loss for class imbalance,
- swarm-based optimization for hyperparameter tuning.

### Main benefits
This combined strategy offers:
- high classification accuracy,
- improved robustness in noisy clinical ECG recordings,
- better detection of subtle waveform abnormalities,
- reduced dependence on manual feature design,
- suitability for automated and potentially real-time diagnosis.

### Broader research trend
The literature shows a strong trend toward integrating **wavelet-domain signal enhancement** with **deep neural architectures**. While some methods use DWT, CWT, or wavelet scattering transforms, DTCWT is especially attractive for arrhythmia detection because of its superior signal representation properties. When paired with CNNs, it supports accurate classification across benchmark datasets such as **MIT-BIH** and related PhysioNet databases.

### Summary
In short, **cardiac arrhythmia detection with dual-tree wavelet transform and CNNs** is a promising approach in which DTCWT improves ECG signal quality and representation, while CNNs automatically learn diagnostic patterns for reliable arrhythmia classification. This combination is well suited for detecting ventricular and supraventricular abnormalities and represents an effective direction for intelligent ECG-based diagnosis.

- Fuzzy control is widely used to handle uncertainty in WSN decisions, especially when inputs such as residual energy, distance, node density, link quality, congestion, and reliability are noisy or conflicting.
- For fault-related operation, fuzzy logic is often paired with energy-aware clustering and routing so that faulty, weak, or unreliable nodes are less likely to be selected for critical roles such as cluster heads or relays.
- Measurement-based techniques continuously monitor parameters like energy consumption, latency, packet delivery ratio, queue size, and link quality, then adapt routing, clustering, or transmission behavior in real time to maintain resilience.
- In fault detection specifically, one framework combines machine learning with energy-efficient fuzzy clustering to detect and classify common sensor faults while reducing energy use and extending network lifetime.
- For fault location or localization under unreliable conditions, robust methods improve position estimation by filtering faulty reference nodes, adapting transmission power, using mobile anchors, trilateration, or multi-round narrowing techniques.

- Fuzzy and possibilistic approaches also help maintain sensing quality despite uncertainty by selecting active nodes and cluster heads based on energy and spatial criteria, which supports reliable monitoring when some nodes are degraded or faulty.
- Congestion-aware fuzzy controllers and adaptive transmission schemes further reduce secondary faults such as packet loss, instability, and excessive retransmissions.

Overall, for the topic fault location measurement sensor nodes fuzzy control algorithm wireless sensor networks, the literature suggests a unified direction: use real-time measurement of node and network conditions, apply fuzzy logic to interpret uncertain inputs, and integrate localization, clustering, routing, and fault-filtering mechanisms to identify faulty nodes or faulty position estimates while preserving energy efficiency, coverage, reliability, and network lifetime.

paragraph_predictions.paragraph:
Multi-script handwritten digit recognition focuses on classifying handwritten numerals across different writing systems and script styles using neural-network-based character classification models. Across the literature, convolutional neural networks are the dominant approach because they learn spatial features directly from images and generally outperform traditional methods such as SVM, K-NN, bag-of-features pipelines, and shallow MLPs on handwritten character and digit tasks. Results reported for scripts such as Devanagari, Telugu, Bangla, Arabic, Sindhi, Amharic, Tibetan, Ethiopic, and multilingual OCR settings consistently show that deep models are effective when supported by good preprocessing, augmentation, and suitable architectures.

A major theme is that model design should match the complexity of the task. For isolated digit or numeral classification, relatively simple CNNs often perform extremely well and may even outperform larger pretrained architectures like GoogLeNet, ResNet-50, or VGG in efficiency or accuracy when datasets are small or visually simple. For more complex handwritten inputs involving multiple scripts, historical documents, mixed-language text, or sequential character streams, hybrid models that combine CNNs with BLSTM/RNN layers, Transformers, attention, and CTC decoding are preferred because they capture both local visual structure and sequence dependencies without explicit segmentation.

Multi-task learning appears as a useful strategy for improving handwritten character recognition, especially when scripts contain structured relationships among classes. One example is Amharic recognition, where a CNN jointly predicts the main character label along with auxiliary row and column positions in the alphabet. This improves generalization by forcing the network to learn informative shared representations. Related work on online handwriting combines classification and trajectory regression losses, showing that multi-task objectives can improve both recognition accuracy and output quality. These findings suggest that for multi-script handwritten digit or character classification, auxiliary tasks such as script identification, style recognition, stroke modeling, or structural attribute prediction can strengthen the main classifier.

Transfer learning and few-shot learning are also important for multi-script settings where labeled data are limited. Fine-tuned pretrained CNNs, style-transfer recognition systems, and few-shot prototypes such as SynergiProtoNet show strong performance across Bangla and Tibetan tasks. These approaches are particularly valuable when expanding recognition systems to new scripts, new writing styles, or low-resource numeral sets without collecting large annotated datasets.

Preprocessing and augmentation remain critical. Common steps include grayscale conversion, resizing, normalization, noise reduction, centering, and sometimes wavelet-based feature extraction. Augmentation through rotations, zooming, distortion, shifting, noise injection, and perspective changes improves robustness to writer variability and document quality. In multilingual and low-quality OCR scenarios, synthetic distortions help models generalize better to blur, noise, and degraded handwriting.

Overall, the literature suggests that an effective multi-script handwritten digit recognition system should combine:  
1. CNN-based visual feature extraction for character classification,  
2. multi-task learning to exploit script structure or auxiliary supervision,  
3. transfer/few-shot learning for low-resource scripts, and  
4. strong preprocessing and augmentation for cross-writer and cross-script robustness.  

For isolated numeral recognition, lightweight CNNs may be sufficient. For mixed-script, sequential, or document-level recognition, CNN-RNN-CTC or CNN-Transformer hybrids are more suitable.

The supplied claims describe this as inductive transfer from the related script-classification task to digit classification.
Character grouping as auxiliary information: For Amharic characters, the alphabet can be organized according to row and column positions.
Predicting these groupings provides easier auxiliary tasks whose structural relationships help the model generalize and improve individual-character recognition.
This illustrates how known relationships among characters can serve a similar role to script identity.

Using auxiliary predictions for regularization: Rather than simply combining several independently weighted losses, the described approach reformulates auxiliary information into a four-class classification problem and uses auxiliary-task predictions to control the main task's loss.
According to the supplied claims, this provides a regularizing mechanism while avoiding the need to manually tune relative loss weights.
Thus, the common idea is to expose the recognizer to related, structured information about each symbol, such as which script it belongs to or which character group it occupies.
Learning these related tasks can constrain the representation toward features useful beyond memorizing individual classes, thereby improving generalization.

Structuring the auxiliary tasks so that their predictions regulate the main loss can also remove a common practical burden of conventional multi-task learning: extensive hyperparameter tuning to determine how strongly each task's loss should be weighted.

Evidence caveat: The supplied metadata marks Multi-script handwritten digit recognition using multi-task learning, which provides several of the specific claims about script classification, four-class reformulation, auxiliary-loss control, and elimination of loss-weight tuning, as retracted.
Those particular findings should therefore not be treated as reliable evidence.
The separate supplied Amharic-character work nevertheless supports the more general claim that auxiliary row/column character-group predictions can improve generalization and recognition accuracy.

paragraph_predictions.paragraph:
A multi-task learning (MTL) approach can improve multi-script handwritten digit recognition through inductive transfer: the model learns the primary task, identifying the digit, together with a related auxiliary task, such as identifying the script. Because the paper Multi-script handwritten digit recognition using multi-task learning is in your retracted-paper list, its specific reported results should not be treated as reliable evidence, but the underlying MTL mechanism can still be explained conceptually.

How the inductive transfer works

Suppose an input image contains a handwritten digit. Instead of training a network only to predict its numerical identity, an MTL model can jointly learn:

Main task: Which digit is this? For example, 0 through 9.
Auxiliary task: Which writing system or script produced it? For example, Arabic, Devanagari, Bengali, or another script.

A simplified architecture is:

Handwritten image
       ↓
 Shared feature extractor
       ↓
  Shared representation
    ↙          ↘
Digit head    Script head
  0–9        Script A/B/...


During training, gradients from both tasks update the shared feature extractor. Script classification therefore supplies an additional learning signal that encourages the representation to capture characteristics useful for distinguishing handwriting across scripts.

Why this can improve digit recognition

1. The auxiliary task provides useful inductive bias.
 Digit appearance is strongly affected by the script in which it is written. Learning to distinguish scripts encourages the feature extractor to encode script-dependent structures, such as characteristic strokes, curvature, orientation, and spatial arrangement. Those features can also help resolve ambiguous digit shapes.

2. Knowledge is transferred between related tasks.
 The benefit is not that script classification directly gives the digit label. Rather, representations learned for script recognition can also be informative for digit classification. This sharing of useful representations is the essence of inductive transfer.

3. The auxiliary objective can act as a regularizer.
 A model optimized exclusively for digit labels may learn features that work well on its training set but generalize poorly. Requiring its internal representation to support another meaningful prediction constrains what it learns:

L=Ldigit+λLscript\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{digit} + \lambda\mathcal{L}_{script}

where λ\lambda controls the auxiliary task's influence. This can discourage overly task-specific representations and reduce overfitting.

4. It can help particularly with visually ambiguous digits.
 Imagine that two scripts render the same numerical digit quite differently, or that a digit in one script resembles another digit in another script. A representation carrying information about both shape and script context gives the digit classifier additional information with which to disambiguate the input.

Important caveat about the supplied evidence

The particular paper associated with the claim, “Multi-script handwritten digit recognition using multi-task learning,” is explicitly identified as retracted in the metadata you supplied. Consequently, claims that its proposed architecture demonstrated superior accuracy, eliminated loss-weight tuning, or experimentally outperformed conventional MTL should not be presented as established evidence based on that article.

So the appropriately qualified conclusion is:

Conceptually, multi-task learning can improve multi-script digit recognition by jointly learning digit and script-related objectives. The auxiliary task supplies an inductive bias that can make shared features more informative and regularize the primary classifier. However, the specific performance improvements reported by the cited retracted study should not be relied upon without verification from independent, non-retracted research.

This distinction separates the general, well-motivated MTL mechanism from the empirical claims of the retracted paper.

paragraph_predictions.paragraph:
Artificial intelligence for commodity image recognition is increasingly driven by deep learning and neural network methods because these models can learn hierarchical visual features directly from raw images and outperform traditional hand-engineered pipelines in complex recognition tasks. Across the literature, convolutional neural networks remain the dominant backbone, using convolution, pooling, and fully connected layers to transform pixel data into semantic representations for classification, detection, and segmentation. More advanced architectures, including ResNet-style residual networks, MobileNet, AlexNet variants, transformers, attention mechanisms, and multimodal hybrids, further improve recognition performance, efficiency, and adaptability.

For commodity image recognition specifically, the evidence suggests that robust systems benefit from combining multiple visual cues such as shape, texture, color, and contextual information. Earlier approaches relied on segmentation and manually extracted descriptors such as texture matrices or PCA-based feature reduction, often followed by classifiers like KNN, SVM, or shallow neural networks. While these methods can still be useful in small-data settings, deep learning offers stronger generalization because it reduces dependence on manual feature selection and can operate effectively in more realistic scenes with cluttered or variable backgrounds. This is especially important for commodity recognition in agriculture, food, spice, and market products, where appearance varies due to lighting, packaging, orientation, size, occlusion, and environmental conditions.

Robustness analysis in this area centers on several recurring factors. First, dataset quality and diversity strongly determine model reliability. Many studies note that limited, imbalanced, or insufficiently representative datasets reduce generalizability, especially when commodities differ across regions, storage conditions, or imaging devices. Data augmentation, transfer learning, self-supervised learning, few-shot learning, and federated learning are therefore highlighted as practical solutions for improving robustness when labeled data are scarce. Second, model robustness depends on architecture choice: deeper or multi-layer neural networks often extract richer features, while lightweight models such as MobileNet and ShuffleNet enable deployment on edge and mobile devices without excessive computational cost. Third, robustness improves when systems fuse complementary information, such as combining texture and shape, integrating multimodal clinical-style data analogs, or using hybrid frameworks that join deep models with classical preprocessing or segmentation methods.

Another major theme is explainability and trustworthiness. Explainable AI techniques such as Grad-CAM and SHAP are repeatedly used to visualize model attention and identify influential features, helping verify that predictions are based on meaningful commodity characteristics rather than background artifacts. This is valuable for robustness assessment because it reveals failure modes, bias, and sensitivity to nuisance factors. Similarly, ablation studies, cross-validation, hyperparameter optimization, and external testing are important for evaluating whether performance gains come from genuine feature learning rather than overfitting.

Overall, the literature supports the view that deep learning-based neural networks provide a strong foundation for commodity image recognition, especially when robustness is addressed through diverse datasets, transfer learning, lightweight yet expressive architectures, feature fusion, and explainability tools. Future progress is likely to come from multimodal learning, self-supervised and few-shot methods, standardized benchmarks, and deployment-ready models that remain accurate under real-world variation.

The provided literature surveys how artificial intelligence and deep neural networks, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs), can be applied to commodity image recognition, with an emphasis on recognition accuracy, generalization, and robustness. Importantly, the paper “Analysis of the role and robustness of artificial intelligence in commodity image recognition under deep learning neural network” is identified in the supplied metadata as retracted, so its specific experimental findings should not be treated as reliable evidence.

The retracted study proposed a multi-stage convolutional neural network (MS-CNN) for recognizing commodities under challenging imaging conditions. It reported that architectural and hyperparameter choices, including 2×2 or 3×3 convolution kernels and a dropout rate of 0.1, improved model performance, with a claimed average recognition accuracy of approximately 97.8%. The study further reported robustness experiments involving corrupted labels and noisy images. According to its claims, recognition accuracy remained above 96% with a 12% label-error probability, while performance under different signal-to-noise ratios exceeded that of the comparison stochastic-gradient method, including a reported peak accuracy of 99.3% at SNR = 0.

The work also evaluated recognition in more realistic commodity-image scenarios, including partial occlusion, changes in viewpoint, different backgrounds, and variations in illumination. Its MS-CNN-based recognition platform was reported to achieve an overall accuracy of 97.1% and a recall rate of 92.9%, with claimed improvements over SIFT, VGG19, and ResNet-based alternatives. Taken at face value, these experiments were intended to demonstrate that multi-stage feature extraction could make commodity recognition less sensitive to image degradation and labeling imperfections.

At a broader level, the underlying technical ideas are consistent with themes appearing throughout the other literature supplied. CNNs learn hierarchical visual representations directly from pixels, reducing dependence on handcrafted descriptors such as SIFT. Deep and residual architectures can improve representation of objects across changes in appearance, while transfer learning, augmentation, lightweight architectures, self-supervised learning, and hybrid approaches can help address limited training data, computational constraints, and distribution shifts. Robust commodity recognition therefore depends not only on nominal test accuracy but also on performance under noise, occlusion, illumination changes, viewpoint variation, background clutter, and imperfect labels.

Overall assessment

The appropriate conclusion is therefore more cautious than the retracted paper's numerical results suggest. Deep neural networks, especially CNN-based architectures, provide a strong general framework for commodity image recognition and can be designed for robustness to real-world visual variation. However, the specific MS-CNN performance figures and superiority claims supplied here originate from a retracted publication and should not be used as validated evidence. Any conclusions about the proposed MS-CNN should instead be independently reproduced using trustworthy datasets, clearly specified baselines, controlled corruption tests, and metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, robustness curves, and uncertainty estimates.

In short: the literature supports deep learning as an important approach to robust image recognition, but the particular claims of 97.1% accuracy, 97.8% average accuracy, 99.3% accuracy at SNR = 0, and >96% accuracy under 12% label corruption should be regarded as unverified because their source has been retracted.

Deep neural networks and deep reinforcement learning are increasingly used to solve wireless communication optimization and resource allocation problems that are hard to address with classical methods alone, especially in dynamic, high-dimensional, and non-convex network environments. Across 5G, beyond-5G, and emerging 6G systems, these methods are applied to allocate power, spectrum, bandwidth, scheduling blocks, beamforming vectors, RIS phase shifts, edge computing resources, and virtualized network functions under strict constraints on latency, reliability, throughput, energy efficiency, fairness, and privacy.

A central theme is that DRL enables adaptive decision-making without requiring complete prior knowledge of traffic or channel statistics. Algorithms such as DQN, DDQN, DDPG, TD3, PPO, and SAC are widely used depending on whether the action space is discrete, continuous, or mixed. SAC is highlighted as particularly effective in complex continuous-control settings such as RIS-assisted vehicular networks, where it jointly optimizes channel sharing, power allocation, and RIS phase control while improving age of information and V2V payload success. PPO is often favored for stable policy updates in heterogeneous RANs, Massive MIMO, semantic-aware V2X, and O-RAN xApps, where it balances throughput, fairness, energy efficiency, and QoS. DDQN and related value-based methods remain effective for scheduling, network slicing, MEC offloading, and V2X channel-power allocation.

Deep neural networks strengthen these RL systems by extracting useful structure from complex wireless states. CNNs and hybrid CNN-RNN models help capture spatial and temporal traffic patterns for 6G resource management. Graph neural networks are especially important when the network topology matters, such as V2X communications, virtual network embedding, and VNF placement, because they encode interference relations, connectivity, and resource dependencies more naturally than standard dense networks. In several works, GNNs combined with DRL improve scalability, reduce observation dimensionality, and support distributed decision-making.

Another major direction is hybrid learning-plus-optimization design. Instead of replacing optimization theory entirely, some frameworks use domain knowledge to decompose difficult problems, reduce decision variables, or derive optimality conditions, and then use DRL only for the intractable parts. This leads to lower complexity, less training data, and near-optimal performance, as shown in ultra-reliable wireless networked control systems. Similar hybrid approaches combine deep learning with metaheuristics or specialized optimization modules for joint power-delay control and other multi-objective wireless problems.

Federated and distributed DRL are also emerging as key tools for scalable wireless optimization. In UAV-assisted cellular systems, NOMA-MEC, wireless powered MEC, and cloud-native wireless networks, federated DRL reduces raw data exchange, improves privacy, and can even outperform centralized learning by enabling collaborative model training across distributed agents or edge devices. These approaches are especially relevant when communication overhead, local data heterogeneity, and privacy constraints limit centralized training.

The application areas are broad. In vehicular and IoV networks, DRL supports AoI-aware allocation, semantic-aware coexistence, anti-interference control, and distributed V2X resource selection. In Massive MIMO and heterogeneous RANs, DRL optimizes energy efficiency, spectral efficiency, fairness, user scheduling, and antenna activation. In MEC and cloud-native systems, it manages offloading, bandwidth sharing, latency minimization, and slice-aware orchestration. In ISAC and anti-jamming scenarios, game-guided DRL combines communication and sensing goals while reacting to adversarial behavior. In network virtualization, hierarchical DRL handles admission control and resource mapping for virtual network requests and service chains.

Overall, the literature shows that deep neural network-based DRL can outperform heuristic, stochastic, and some conventional optimization baselines in convergence speed, cumulative reward, throughput, latency, reliability, AoI, energy efficiency, and fairness. At the same time, recurring challenges remain: computational complexity, scalability to very large networks, non-stationary environments, reward design, training stability, data scarcity, privacy, and the gap between simulation and real deployment. Current trends point toward more structured models using GNNs and transformers, more scalable federated and hierarchical DRL, integration with optimization theory, and exploration of quantum-enhanced learning for future 6G resource management.

Summary: Deep Neural Networks and Deep Reinforcement Learning for Wireless Communication Resource Optimization

Deep neural networks (DNNs) and deep reinforcement learning (DRL) are increasingly used to address complex resource-allocation and optimization problems in wireless networks. By learning from high-dimensional network states and adapting decisions to changing channel, traffic, mobility, and interference conditions, these approaches can optimize resources such as spectrum, transmit power, bandwidth, scheduling blocks, antennas, beamforming, computing capacity, and task offloading. Reinforcement-learning approaches including DQN, DDQN, PPO, SAC, TD3, and hierarchical or federated DRL are particularly suited to sequential decisions where conventional optimization can become computationally expensive.

Across the supplied studies, DRL is applied to a broad range of architectures, including cognitive radio, 5G/6G network slicing, Massive MIMO, V2X and RIS-assisted vehicular networks, UAV-assisted cellular systems, O-RAN, MEC, NOMA, cloud-native wireless networks, and integrated sensing and communication. The general formulation represents resource management as a Markov decision process: network measurements form the state, allocation choices form the actions, and rewards capture objectives such as throughput, spectral efficiency, energy efficiency, latency, reliability, fairness, AoI, or combinations of these criteria. DNNs provide the function approximation necessary to deal with large state and action spaces.

A recurring theme is multi-objective optimization. Rather than maximizing throughput alone, recent approaches jointly consider energy and spectral efficiency, latency and reliability, fairness, interference, or sensing and communication performance. Several studies further combine DRL with complementary techniques such as graph neural networks for topology-aware decisions, optimization theory for reducing the learning search space, federated learning for distributed and privacy-preserving training, game theory for anti-jamming decisions, and semantic communications for more efficient use of spectrum. Such hybrid designs can improve scalability and reduce the need to exchange raw network data.

Reported simulation and experimental findings in the supplied material generally indicate that appropriately designed DRL methods can outperform heuristic, traditional DQN, or conventional optimization baselines, particularly under dynamic and uncertain network conditions. Benefits include faster or more stable convergence, improved spectrum and energy utilization, reduced latency, better reliability, and adaptation to mobility and fluctuating network demand. This suggests a progression from static resource optimization toward adaptive, context-aware and near-real-time network control, including deployment through O-RAN xApps and edge/cloud-native architectures.

However, these results should not be treated uniformly. Practical deployment remains constrained by training cost, computational complexity, data availability, scalability, reward design, generalization to unseen conditions, security vulnerabilities, and the gap between simulation and operational networks. Performance also depends strongly on state/action representation, network assumptions, QoS constraints, and the selected DRL algorithm.

Retraction caveat

Importantly, the supplied metadata identifies “Application of deep neural network and deep reinforcement learning in wireless communication” as retracted. Its specific claims about intelligent power control, DQN convergence, spectrum sharing, near-100% success rates, and superiority of particular power-control strategies therefore should not be used as reliable supporting evidence. The broader conclusion that DNN/DRL methods are promising for wireless resource allocation can instead be evaluated from the other, non-retracted studies in the supplied corpus.

Overall, the literature represented here positions DNN and DRL as flexible tools for transforming wireless resource allocation from fixed, model-dependent optimization into adaptive learning-based control. The strongest direction appears to be hybrid and distributed DRL, combining neural decision-making with optimization theory, GNNs, federated learning, RIS, semantic communication, or game-theoretic mechanisms to meet the increasingly heterogeneous requirements of 5G, 6G, IoT, vehicular, edge, and O-RAN networks.

Consolidated overlapping claims into common themes rather than treating every paper separately.

Highlighted both reported advantages and practical limitations.

paragraph_predictions.paragraph:
Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) can serve as an adaptive control mechanism for power, channel, scheduling, and related radio-resource decisions in wireless networks whose channel conditions, interference patterns, traffic demands, mobility, and service requirements change over time. The supplied evidence also shows that the policy learned by DRL is strongly determined by its reward and constraints: changing the priority among interference, freshness, reliability, latency, and efficiency changes what resource-allocation behavior is desirable.

Adaptive power and channel allocation

Across the supplied studies, DRL is used to learn resource-allocation policies through interaction with dynamic network environments rather than relying entirely on fixed allocation rules or prior knowledge of system statistics. Examples include:

Joint channel and power selection: In vehicular networks, GNN-DDQN methods optimize channel and power choices while adapting to changing vehicle densities and interference relationships.
Power plus scheduling/resource blocks: DDQN-based network slicing jointly assigns transmission power and scheduling blocks for services with different QoS requirements.
Joint control of several coupled resources: SAC-based vehicular allocation simultaneously controls channel sharing, transmit power, and RIS phase shifts, while PPO-based Massive MIMO control dynamically manages power allocation, user scheduling, and antenna activation.
Adversarial or interference-varying environments: Game-guided DRL jointly adapts channel selection and power control in response to jamming and inter-channel interference.
Near-real-time operation: DRL-based O-RAN controllers optimize transmit power, bandwidth slicing, and scheduling, illustrating how a learned policy can support continuing adaptation rather than a one-time static optimization.

The evidence therefore portrays DRL as particularly useful when the allocation problem is dynamic, high-dimensional, coupled, or difficult to solve directly as a conventional optimization problem.

How the objective shapes the learned policy

1. Interference avoidance

When interference reduction is part of the objective or operational requirements, the learned policy is pushed toward channel and power decisions that limit harmful interactions between links. In V2X communications, for example, resource allocation seeks to maintain V2V communication success while minimizing interference to V2I links. In ISAC systems facing jamming, DRL adjusts both channel selection and transmit power to mitigate jamming and inter-channel interference.

Thus, interference avoidance does not necessarily mean simply minimizing transmit power. The policy has to find allocations that preserve useful communication while selecting channels and power levels that control interference.

2. Timely information delivery

When timeliness is important, simply maximizing throughput is insufficient. The AoI-aware vehicular work explicitly minimizes Age of Information (AoI) on V2I links while also improving V2V payload-transmission success. Its SAC policy jointly optimizes channel sharing, power allocation, and RIS configuration in a high-mobility environment.

Similarly, network-slicing rewards can be differentiated by service: eMBB rewards favor throughput, whereas URLLC rewards emphasize low delay and high reliability. Ultra-reliable wireless control likewise incorporates packet-delay and transfer-interval constraints alongside communication-resource decisions.

Consequently, a freshness- or latency-oriented reward encourages the agent to allocate resources according to when information must arrive, rather than purely according to instantaneous rate or resource efficiency.

3. Transmission success and reliability

Reliability objectives make successful delivery a direct determinant of allocations. The supplied work connects packet-transmission success probability with signal power and channel quality, allowing resource decisions to reflect the relationship between power and successful transmission. Other vehicular approaches explicitly seek high V2V communication success rates while satisfying latency and reliability requirements.

This creates an inherent balancing problem: allocating additional power or favorable channels can improve the probability of successful transmission, but those decisions can also affect interference, energy consumption, and resources available to other links.

Overall interpretation

The common theme is that DRL provides a way to turn these competing requirements into an adaptive control policy:

network observations → learned policy → channel/power/resource decisions → performance feedback → policy optimized toward the specified reward and constraints

The resulting policy therefore depends critically on what is rewarded and constrained. An interference-oriented policy favors allocations that protect other links; an AoI- or latency-oriented policy favors decisions supporting timely delivery; a reliability-oriented policy prioritizes successful packets; and multi-objective formulations seek compromises among reliability, throughput, spectrum efficiency, energy efficiency, fairness, and delay.

Importantly, the supplied studies do not establish one universally optimal DRL policy or objective. Rather, they collectively indicate that DRL's role is to learn adaptive decisions for the particular operating conditions and service goals encoded in the optimization problem. Interference avoidance

Joint power and radio-resource allocation: DQN and particularly Double DQN (DDQN) can jointly select transmit-power levels and scheduling blocks. In network slicing, DDQN-based allocation combines resource reservation and sharing with slice-specific reward functions. This allows eMBB traffic to emphasize throughput, while URLLC traffic emphasizes low packet delay and high reliability. The reported approach improves delay, throughput, energy efficiency, and processing time relative to distributed and equal-sharing baselines.

Reliability-aware power decisions: Packet-transmission success probability can be related to transmission power and channel-quality indicators, allowing the DRL agent's decisions or rewards to account explicitly for reliability. Optimization-theory-assisted DQN/DDQN approaches can additionally incorporate constraints involving packet error probability, blocklength, packet delay, and control-system stability, enabling power minimization while maintaining ultra-reliable transmission.

Interference-aware spectrum reuse: DRL agents can jointly choose channels and transmit powers according to observed network conditions. In vehicular networks, combining graph neural networks with DDQN supports distributed channel and power selection that maintains V2V reliability and latency requirements while reducing interference to V2I links and improving V2I transmission rates. The graph representation also helps agents adapt as vehicle density and network topology change.

Dynamic spectrum and channel management: Reinforcement learning learns resource-allocation policies through repeated interaction with its environment rather than requiring prior knowledge of all system statistics. This makes it applicable to changing channels, traffic loads, mobility, and interference. In high-mobility vehicular settings, DRL has been used to jointly optimize channel sharing and power allocation, together with RIS phase shifts, improving information freshness and payload transmission success.

Spectrum and energy efficiency: Multi-objective DRL can incorporate several network objectives into its reward or optimization target. For UAV-assisted cellular networks, a UCB-based dueling DDQN jointly optimizes beamforming and power allocation to improve combined spectrum and energy efficiency, with faster convergence than conventional DQN methods. Massive-MIMO work similarly indicates that dynamic power allocation, user scheduling, and antenna activation can balance spectral efficiency, energy efficiency, throughput, and resource utilization.

Delay-sensitive allocation and offloading: DQN can extend resource management beyond radio transmission itself. In cloud-native wireless networks, DQN-based task-offloading decisions reduce MEC task-processing latency, while other DRL methods allocate bandwidth using objectives based on latency, transmission rate, and service type. Federated DDQN has also been applied jointly to offloading, base-station assignment, channel allocation, computing resources, and transmit-power control for reducing delivery latency and energy consumption under QoS requirements.

Anti-jamming and interference management: Power control can be formulated as a Markov decision process and combined with channel selection. Game-guided DRL has been reported to adapt channel and power choices to malicious jamming and inter-channel interference, improving communication and sensing performance and responding dynamically to jammer behavior.

Near-real-time RAN control: DRL policies can be implemented in near-real-time RAN controllers to optimize transmit power, bandwidth slicing, user scheduling, and slicing policies. The supplied evidence also indicates that control timescales and reward design matter: telemetry intervals, action-update frequency, and reward weights can change throughput and the balance of QoS across eMBB, mMTC, and URLLC services.

Practical formulation

Taken together, these results suggest treating wireless resource management as a sequential decision problem:

Network observations such as channel conditions, interference, traffic demand, mobility, resource availability, and QoS state
 → DQN/DDQN or another DRL policy
 → actions such as power level, channel, scheduling block, bandwidth, beamforming, or offloading choice
 → reward and constraints reflecting throughput, spectrum/energy efficiency, packet reliability, latency, and interference
 → continuous policy adaptation as network conditions evolve.

For discrete radio decisions, DQN/DDQN is particularly applicable to choices such as channels, scheduling blocks, and quantized power levels. Other DRL methods in the supplied material, including SAC, PPO, TD3, and DDPG-based approaches, are used when the resource-allocation problem involves different or more complex action spaces.

Overall, the supplied evidence supports DRL as an adaptive framework for coordinating power, spectrum, scheduling, and interference decisions rather than optimizing each independently. The reported benefits include better spectrum/resource utilization, higher throughput and packet success, lower delay, stronger reliability, and improved interference management. Hybrid approaches that incorporate optimization theory, graph representations, federated learning, or game-theoretic structure can further address constraints, network topology, scalability/privacy, and adversarial interference.

Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) can optimize spectrum sharing by learning adaptive policies that jointly control channel access, transmit power, scheduling, bandwidth, beamforming, and related radio parameters as network conditions and user loads change. Across the supplied evidence, several complementary mechanisms emerge for increasing spectrum efficiency while controlling interference and congestion.

Joint channel and power allocation: DRL can select channels and power levels together rather than treating them independently. In vehicular networks, SAC-based optimization jointly manages channel sharing, power allocation, and RIS phase shifts, while GNN-DDQN approaches optimize channel and power selection to maintain V2V reliability and improve V2I rates while minimizing interference to V2I links.

Interference-aware state representations: Graph neural networks can complement DRL by representing communication and interference relationships among users. Limiting each node's neighborhood to important communication relationships preserves strong interference relationships while keeping computation manageable in dense networks. This supports distributed decisions by individual users without ignoring the broader interference structure.

Coexistence mechanisms: For heterogeneous users sharing unlicensed spectrum, a DRL-controlled flexible duty cycle can coordinate access opportunities. The supplied 5G-V2X evidence indicates that jointly optimizing duty-cycle coexistence and resource allocation for vehicular and WiFi users can improve semantic spectrum efficiency, with semantic communication also reported to reduce congestion relative to conventional bit-based approaches.

Adaptive scheduling and slicing: DDQN can jointly allocate transmit power and scheduling blocks among network slices. Combining learning with resource reservation and resource sharing allows resources to be shifted between heterogeneous services while preserving their different QoS objectives. Slice-specific reward functions can favor throughput for eMBB while prioritizing low delay and reliability for URLLC. Similarly, DRL-based Open RAN control can coordinate slicing and scheduling, including hierarchical decisions at different timescales.

Multi-objective reward design: Spectrum efficiency need not be optimized in isolation. PPO-based Massive MIMO resource allocation jointly adjusts power, user scheduling, and antenna activation using rewards that balance energy and spectral efficiency. UAV-assisted approaches similarly combine spectrum and energy efficiency and jointly optimize beamforming and power. In heterogeneous networks, multi-objective policies can balance throughput, fairness, and energy consumption.

Constraint-aware DRL: Explicit constraints provide a mechanism for preventing efficiency gains from violating service requirements. The supplied work includes constrained DRL that satisfies latency and reliability constraints, and optimization-theory-guided DRL that minimizes power while enforcing reliability, packet-delay, and control-stability requirements.

Anti-interference and anti-jamming control: A game-guided DRL framework combines Stackelberg-game channel selection with DRL-based power control. This allows adaptation to jammer behavior while mitigating inter-channel interference and balancing communication rate with sensing performance.

Distributed and federated learning: Federated DRL enables users or network entities to learn collaboratively without exchanging raw data. The supplied studies associate this approach with scalability, reduced data exchange, privacy preservation, and efficient resource allocation in UAV, MEC, and IoT settings.

Overall, the evidence supports a design in which DRL observes changing channels, interference, traffic, user relationships, and service requirements, then dynamically chooses coupled resource-allocation actions. Spectrum efficiency is improved not simply by maximizing utilization, but by pairing learning with interference-aware graph representations, adaptive power control, flexible coexistence duty cycles, scheduling and reservation policies, carefully constructed multi-objective rewards, QoS constraints, and, where appropriate, game-theoretic or federated mechanisms.

One supplied paper, Application of deep neural network and deep reinforcement learning in wireless communication, is explicitly listed as retracted in the provided metadata. Its claims about cognitive-radio spectrum sharing and primary/secondary-user power control therefore should not be relied upon as supporting evidence; the conclusions above are instead grounded in the other supplied claims.

paragraph_predictions.paragraph:
Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) can adaptively manage transmit power and radio resources by treating network operation as a sequential decision problem: the agent observes changing channel, traffic, interference, mobility, and service conditions, then continually selects power and resource-allocation actions to optimize a reward while respecting reliability, latency, or interference constraints.

Based on the supplied evidence, an effective approach has several components:

Jointly control power and radio resources. Rather than optimizing transmit power in isolation, DRL can jointly select power levels, channels or scheduling blocks, bandwidth, user schedules, beamforming parameters, antenna activation, and related controls. DDQN has been used for joint power and scheduling-block allocation in network slicing, while PPO has dynamically managed power allocation, user scheduling, and antenna activation in Massive MIMO. In UAV-assisted cellular networks, UCB-based DDQN jointly optimizes beamforming and power allocation.

Make spectral efficiency part of the learning objective. The reward can explicitly balance spectrum utilization against other objectives. In Massive MIMO, a unified reward combining energy and spectral efficiency allows PPO to adapt this trade-off as network conditions change. Multi-objective DRL for UAV-assisted cellular networks similarly combines spectrum and energy efficiency into an optimization objective and reports higher weighted energy-spectrum efficiency than conventional DQN approaches.

Control interference through the state, actions, and objective. DRL can learn channel and power decisions that account for interfering links rather than simply increasing transmit power. A GNN-DDQN approach for V2X communications jointly optimizes channel and power selection while minimizing interference to V2I links and satisfying V2V latency and reliability requirements. For integrated sensing and communications, game-guided DDPG jointly controls channel selection and base-station transmit power to mitigate inter-channel interference and malicious jamming.

Encode QoS requirements directly into optimization. Slice-specific rewards can make eMBB agents favor throughput while making URLLC agents minimize delay and maximize reliability. Resource reservation and sharing can then complement DRL to allocate power and scheduling blocks across slices. Other supplied work shows constrained DRL using an additional critic to enforce latency and reliability-related constraints, illustrating how constraints can be incorporated rather than treated only as soft performance goals.

Use network context for adaptation. An MDP formulation can expose relevant conditions such as channel quality, interference geometry, traffic/service type, mobility, and available resources to the agent. For heterogeneous networks, a Near-RT RIC xApp uses DRL to adjust transmit power, bandwidth slicing, and scheduling, while an MDP incorporating global channel knowledge and interference geometry supports those decisions. In vehicular networks, GNNs can compress changing interference/connectivity relationships into useful features for distributed DRL decisions.

Operate at appropriate timescales. The supplied O-RAN evidence indicates that telemetry reporting intervals and action-update times materially affect DRL performance, and that hierarchical xApps operating at different timescales can coordinate slicing and scheduling. Thus rapid power/scheduling decisions can be separated from slower resource-partitioning decisions.

The resulting control loop can therefore be summarized as:

observe network conditions → choose joint power/channel/bandwidth/scheduling actions → measure throughput, spectral efficiency, interference and QoS outcomes → compute a multi-objective or constrained reward → update the DRL policy → repeat as conditions change.

The supplied studies suggest several suitable algorithm families, including PPO, DDQN, TD3, SAC, DDPG, GNN-assisted DDQN, and federated DRL. The appropriate choice depends on the decision structure. SAC, for example, is reported to handle high-dimensional state spaces and dynamic decisions in high-mobility vehicular networks, whereas GNN-DDQN supports distributed decisions when interference relationships form a changing graph.

Overall, the evidence supports using DRL not simply as a power controller, but as a context-aware joint resource controller. Spectral efficiency can be improved by learning when and where additional power or spectrum is useful, while interference, latency, reliability, and other QoS requirements are represented through constraints, penalties, or carefully designed multi-objective rewards. The supplied Massive MIMO study, for example, reports DRL optimization with QoS violation rates below 1% across the tested antenna and user configurations.

Retraction handling: I excluded the claims from Application of deep neural network and deep reinforcement learning in wireless communication because that title appears in the supplied retracted-paper metadata.
